passage: Last winter my mother was in hospital for a week, and nobody at home remembered my tiffin. On the first day I sat at lunch pretending I wasn't hungry. Chaitanya noticed. He didn't say anything, just tore his paratha in half and slid it over. The next day he brought two parathas. He did it all week and never told anyone. I only found out later that he'd asked his mother to make extra. I still don't know how to repay that. When I thanked him, he just said, "You'd do it too, Nitin." I hope I would.

qa.q: How long did Chaitanya bring extra food?
qa.a: All week.

qa.q: What does Nitin's "I still don't know how to repay that" show?
qa.a: Nitin feels deeply thankful, knowing Chaitanya went out of his way on purpose to help.

qa.q: What could Nitin do with his gratitude now?
qa.a: Thank Chaitanya's mother too, and look out for someone else in need, as Chaitanya did for Nitin.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have said "You'd do it too"?
qa.a: He may have wanted to keep it simple and not make Nitin feel indebted.

grounding: It shows a child recognising and feeling thankful for a friend's deliberate, quiet kindness.

passage: Teacher's note, Uma, Class 4. This morning Rafiq came to me with a card he'd made himself. Yesterday his cycle chain broke on the way to school, and the bus driver, Mani Anna, stopped, put the cycle in the back and brought him in, even though Rafiq doesn't ride that bus. The card said, "Thank you for stopping. You didn't have to." Rafiq asked if he could give it himself. At dismissal he held it out with both hands. I have asked the class to think of one person who helped them on purpose this week.

qa.q: What happened to Rafiq's cycle?
qa.a: Its chain broke on the way to school.

qa.q: What does "You didn't have to" in Rafiq's card show he understood?
qa.a: He understood that Mani Anna chose to help him out of kindness, not because it was his job.

qa.q: Why is Uma's class activity useful?
qa.a: It helps other children notice kindness done on purpose and feel thankful for it.

qa.q: How might Mani Anna feel receiving the card?
qa.a: Touched and appreciated, since a driver's small kindnesses often go unthanked. 🙏

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a boy recognising an adult's intentional kindness and thanking him.

passage:
Dear Diary,
I missed a whole week of school with fever, and I was so scared about the science test. Today Lavanya came to my house with her notebook. She had written all the notes twice, once for her and once for me, in her neat round handwriting, with little drawings of the heart and lungs. She hadn't even told me she was doing it. I almost cried. I tried to give her my best gel pen and she refused, so I'll make her a bookmark instead. I didn't know someone would do that just for me. 🙏
- Swati

qa.q: What had Lavanya drawn in the notes?
qa.a: Little drawings of the heart and lungs.

qa.q: Why did Swati almost cry?
qa.a: Swati was moved that Lavanya had spent time writing notes just for Swati, without being asked or saying a word about it.

qa.q: What is a good way for Swati to show thanks, since Lavanya refused the pen?
qa.a: A handmade bookmark and a sincere thank-you, which match the care Lavanya put in.

qa.q: Why might Lavanya have refused the gel pen?
qa.a: She probably didn't want payment; she helped because she cared, not to get something back.

grounding: It shows a child feeling thankful for a friend's deliberate, unasked-for kindness.

passage: On the dusty road outside the village, Nilesh's cycle chain snapped on his way to school. He pushed it to Hansa Aunty's small repair shop. She put down her tea, fixed it and waved away his coins. 'Go, you'll be late.' Nilesh stood there a moment, surprised. She hadn't had to do that. All day he kept thinking about it. The next morning he brought her three guavas from his tree, wrapped in newspaper. 'Thank you, Aunty,' he said, and felt warm when she smiled.

qa.q: What did Nilesh bring Hansa Aunty the next morning?
qa.a: He brought her three guavas from his tree, wrapped in newspaper.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh stand there surprised for a moment?
qa.a: He realised Hansa Aunty had chosen to help him for free, and it touched him.

qa.q: What made Nilesh's thank-you meaningful?
qa.a: He gave something of his own and said thank you in person, showing he truly noticed her kindness.

qa.q: How might Hansa Aunty feel receiving the guavas?
qa.a: She would likely feel appreciated and happy that her small act meant something to him. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising and feeling thankful for an intentional act of kindness, in rural India.

passage: When Vera's cat went missing in their Prague apartment building, their neighbour Gabriel spent an hour searching the stairwells with a torch. He found the cat stuck behind a boiler in the basement. That night Vera couldn't sleep. She kept thinking how Gabriel didn't have to help; he'd just come home from work. The next day she made a card with a drawing of the cat and wrote, 'Thank you for finding Mishka. You are very kind.' She slid it under his door and ran back upstairs, heart thumping.

qa.q: Where did Gabriel find the cat?
qa.a: He found it stuck behind a boiler in the basement.

qa.q: Why did Vera keep thinking about Gabriel's help?
qa.a: She felt grateful because she understood he chose to help even though he was tired after work.

qa.q: What could Vera do if she wants to thank Gabriel even more?
qa.a: She could say thank you in person next time she sees him, adding to her card.

qa.q: How might Gabriel feel when he finds the card?
qa.a: He would likely be touched and glad his effort mattered to Vera.

grounding: Shows a child recognising a neighbour's intentional kindness and expressing gratitude, set in the Czech Republic.

passage: The hostel was cold that January, and Farhan, ten, had forgotten his sweater at home. He shivered through study hour. Tejas, from the next bed, said nothing but came back with his own spare sweater and put it on Farhan's desk. That evening Farhan also found Tejas had copied the maths notes he'd missed. Farhan held the sweater for a moment. "You didn't have to," he said. Tejas shrugged. "You'd do it." Farhan wrote him a note that night: "Thank you. I won't forget."

qa.q: What had Farhan forgotten at home?
qa.a: His sweater.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he held the sweater for a moment?
qa.a: He felt grateful and touched that Tejas had noticed and helped without being asked.

qa.q: What could Farhan do to show his gratitude?
qa.a: Thank Tejas, as he did, and look for ways to help Tejas in return.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel reading Farhan's note?
qa.a: Warm and valued, glad his kindness mattered.

grounding: Shows a child recognising and thanking a hostel friend for deliberate kindness.

passage: I'm Irfan, Shreya's brother. Last week the school bus driver, Mahesh Uncle, waited five extra minutes when Shreya, who's nine, ran late because her shoe came off. The next day she made a thank-you card with a drawing of the bus and wrote, "Thank you for waiting for me." She gave it to him with a sweet. He smiled and put the card on his dashboard. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she talked about it all evening.

qa.q: How long did Mahesh Uncle wait?
qa.a: Five extra minutes.

qa.q: What might Shreya have been feeling when she made the card?
qa.a: She seemed grateful and warm, wanting to thank him for waiting on purpose.

qa.q: How could Shreya's parents encourage this habit?
qa.a: Notice and praise the card, and help her remember to thank people who help her.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Shreya's gratitude?
qa.a: He notices she talked about it all evening, which suggests it mattered to her.

grounding: Shows a child recognising a bus driver's deliberate kindness and thanking him, seen by her brother.

passage: September: Keerthana, from the next flat, started helping Jeevan, eleven, with fractions every Saturday. He came, but grumbled, checking the clock. October: he still sighed, but he started asking questions. November: the exam results came. Jeevan got his best maths mark ever. That evening he knocked on Keerthana's door with a box of barfi from his mother. "You gave up your Saturdays," he said, looking at his feet. "Thank you." Keerthana grinned. "You gave up yours too."

qa.q: When did Keerthana start helping Jeevan?
qa.a: In September.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan look at his feet when he thanked Keerthana?
qa.a: He felt grateful but a bit shy, maybe sheepish about grumbling before.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to keep showing thanks?
qa.a: Keep working hard and maybe help another student, the way Keerthana helped him.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Jeevan thanks her?
qa.a: Pleased and proud, seeing her Saturdays paid off.

grounding: Shows a child slowly recognising a neighbour's deliberate help and thanking her.

passage: Lakshmi Ammamma settled in her chair. "Urmila, when I was ten, we had no books at home. Our neighbour, Venkatesh Mama, was a clerk and had shelves full. One day he saw me reading an old newspaper on the step. The next Sunday he knocked and handed me a book. 'Return it next week, and I'll give you another.' He did that for two whole years. I didn't have words then for how thankful I was. I just made him a card from a matchbox and drew a book on it. He kept it on his shelf till he died." Urmila touched the old matchbox on the table. "Is this it?" "His son returned it to me."

qa.q: What did young Lakshmi make for Venkatesh Mama?
qa.a: A card from a matchbox with a book drawn on it.

qa.q: How did young Lakshmi feel about Venkatesh Mama's books?
qa.a: She felt deeply thankful and grateful, even without words for it.

qa.q: What was the key moment in the story, and how did young Lakshmi show her thanks?
qa.a: The key moment was the neighbour noticing her reading and bringing her books; she showed thanks with a handmade card.

qa.q: How might Venkatesh Mama have felt about keeping the card?
qa.a: He likely felt touched and appreciated, which is why he kept it for so long.

grounding: A grandmother remembers her gratitude to a neighbour who lent her books as a child.

passage: It was exam day, pouring rain, and Tushar had left his lunch box and his pen at home. He stood at his desk, wet and panicking. Raghav, beside him, silently held out a blue pen. Then, at break, he pushed half his idli across. "I'm not that hungry," he said. But Tushar saw him look at the idli before giving it. Tushar's throat felt tight. After the exam, he found Raghav at the gate. "Thanks, yaar. You didn't have to." Raghav shrugged. "You'd do it." Tushar decided he'd bring extra snacks tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Raghav hold out to Tushar?
qa.a: A blue pen.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he saw Raghav look at the idli before giving it?
qa.a: He felt grateful and touched, understanding that Raghav had given up something he wanted.

qa.q: How did Tushar plan to show his thanks?
qa.a: By bringing extra snacks the next day.

qa.q: How might Raghav see his own kindness?
qa.a: Raghav seems to think of it as normal, something Tushar would also do.

grounding: On a rainy exam day, a boy feels grateful when a classmate shares his pen and lunch.

passage: Karthik broke his wrist falling off his cycle in Kochi and missed a week of school. When he came back, his arm in a cast, Mohit handed him a thick notebook. "I copied all the notes. Science, social studies, maths. Twice, so one's in neat writing." Karthik flipped through. Mohit had even drawn the diagrams. "You did this every night?" "Mostly." Karthik felt a warm lump in his chest. He knew Mohit hated writing. "Thanks. Really." Mohit grinned. "Just don't make me copy the next test."

qa.q: How long did Karthik miss school?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he felt a warm lump in his chest?
qa.a: He felt grateful and moved, knowing Mohit hated writing and had done it for him anyway.

qa.q: How could Karthik return the kindness?
qa.a: He could thank Mohit properly, perhaps help him with a subject he finds hard, or be there when Mohit needs help.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel about his effort being noticed?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and a bit shy, making a joke to cover it.

grounding: A boy feels grateful when a friend copies a week of notes for him after his injury.

passage:
"Samir, here." Zainab put a notebook on his desk.

"What's this?"

"My science notes. You missed three days when you had fever. The test is on Monday."

Samir flipped through. Every page was neat, with diagrams. "You copied all this for me?"

"I made a second copy last night."

"That must have taken hours."

Zainab shrugged. "You'd do it for me."

Samir looked at her. "Thank you. Really. I was so worried about the test."

"Just don't lose it."

qa.q: How many days of school did Samir miss?
qa.a: Samir missed three days when he had fever.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when he saw the notes?
qa.a: Samir felt grateful and relieved, since he had been worried about the test.

qa.q: How could Samir show his gratitude further?
qa.a: He could return the notes on time, help Zainab later, or thank her with a small note.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when Samir thanked her?
qa.a: Zainab likely felt appreciated and happy to have helped.

grounding: A child feels thankful when a classmate spends hours making him a copy of her notes.

passage:
The Diwali I was nine, I tore my new lehenga on the gate just before the puja. I cried so loudly that the neighbours came out.

Kavitha Aunty from next door took one look, went home, and came back with her sewing kit. She sat on our steps under the bulb and fixed it in ten minutes. You could hardly see the stitches.

I remember hugging her so hard she laughed. She didn't have to help. She had her own puja to do.

I'm Shreya, and every Diwali I take Kavitha Aunty the first box of sweets.

qa.q: Where did Shreya tear the lehenga?
qa.a: Shreya tore it on the gate.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Kavitha Aunty fixed the lehenga?
qa.a: Shreya felt deeply grateful and relieved, hugging her tightly.

qa.q: How does Shreya show gratitude now?
qa.a: Every Diwali, Shreya takes Kavitha Aunty the first box of sweets.

qa.q: How might Kavitha Aunty see her act of kindness?
qa.a: Kavitha Aunty probably saw it as a small, natural thing to do, though she had her own puja.

grounding: A child remembers feeling thankful when a neighbour mended a torn Diwali lehenga.

passage:
Teacher's note, monsoon.

Today it poured at home time. Siddharth had forgotten his umbrella. Jomon, who lives in the opposite direction, walked him all the way to his lane under his own umbrella and then walked back alone. His mother told me he reached home soaked.

This morning, Siddharth brought Jomon a drawing of two boys under an umbrella, with "THANK YOU" in big letters. He told the class, "Jomon didn't have to do it."

I've pinned the drawing on the board.

— class teacher

qa.q: What did Siddharth bring Jomon?
qa.a: He brought a drawing of two boys under an umbrella, with "THANK YOU" in big letters.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel about what Jomon did?
qa.a: Siddharth felt grateful, recognising that Jomon chose to help him.

qa.q: How did the teacher encourage gratitude?
qa.a: The teacher pinned the drawing on the board.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about the drawing?
qa.a: Jomon likely felt touched and appreciated.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy expressing gratitude to a classmate who walked him home in the rain.

passage:
Dear Diary, 18 July, still raining
I was home with a cold for three days, and I was dreading Friday's maths test. This evening the doorbell rang, and it was Kavitha from my class, soaking wet, with a plastic bag. Inside were her maths notes, copied out neatly for me, with the hard sums marked in red. She must have done it after school instead of playing. I said thanks, but it didn't feel like enough. After she left I just sat there holding the pages. Tomorrow I'm going to give her my best pencil set and help her with the English poem she hates.
Kunal

qa.q: How many days was Kunal home with a cold?
qa.a: Kunal was home with a cold for three days.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel holding the pages after Kavitha left?
qa.a: Kunal felt deeply grateful and touched, knowing Kavitha had given up playtime to help. 🙏

qa.q: What could Kunal do to show thanks in a way that fits the kindness?
qa.a: Besides the pencil set, Kunal could tell Kavitha exactly how much the notes helped once the test is over.

qa.q: Why might Kavitha have come over in the rain?
qa.a: Kavitha probably cared about Kunal missing lessons and wanted to help before the Friday test.

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising and feeling thankful for a classmate's deliberate kindness during the rains.
